title: Transition to extrauterine life and immediate care
blurb: Support a baby's transition at birth: Apgar scoring, skin-to-skin and warmth, the first feed, and observations after meconium or prolonged rupture of membranes (NICE NG235, RCUK 2025).
question: Baby Amani is born at 39 weeks through thick meconium-stained liquor. He cries at once, has good tone and a heart rate of 140. The student midwife reaches for the suction catheter. What should the midwife advise, and how should Amani be observed?

teach.h: From placenta to lungs in minutes
teach.body: Formally: transition is the baby's adaptation to extrauterine life: lungs aerate and take over gas exchange from the placenta, the circulation changes as pulmonary blood flow rises, and the baby begins to regulate temperature and glucose. In plain English: at birth a baby must breathe, keep warm and start feeding. Most do this unaided. The midwife's job is to support it (warmth, skin-to-skin, airway, early feeding) and spot the few babies who need help.
teach.cite: NMC SPM 3.13.2; RCUK 2025 Newborn resuscitation and support of transition

items.label: Apgar score
items.sub: and record time to regular breathing

head: Sign
What you assess
rows: Absent, weak or irregular, good cry
Look inside the mouth (central) and nail beds (peripheral)
teach.caption: Record at 1 and 5 minutes for all births (NG235 1.11.1). NG235 1.11.2: assess central oxygenation by looking at the mucous membranes and tongue, peripheral at the nail beds.

items: Encourage skin-to-skin as soon as possible; if the woman is not well enough, her birth companion can (NG235 1.11.7).
Dry the baby and cover with a warm, dry towel while keeping skin-to-skin (1.11.8). Aim for a temperature of 36.5-37.5 C (RCUK 2025).
Support the head so the airway stays open; show parents how to keep it clear (1.11.9).
Avoid separation in the first hour for routine weighing, measuring or bathing (1.11.10).
Encourage breastfeeding as soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour (1.11.11). Examinations and treatment with parental consent (1.11.18).

root.label: Any meconium in the liquor
root.sub: do not suction before the shoulders and trunk are born

teach.caption: Significant meconium is dark green or black amniotic fluid that is thick or tenacious, or any meconium-stained fluid with lumps of meconium.

teach.h: Call a neonatologist after any meconium if (NG235 1.11.29)
head: Observation
Trigger
rows: 38 C or above, or 37.5 C twice 15-30 min apart
teach.caption: Transfer both woman and baby if at home or in a freestanding midwifery unit.

teach.body: Amani is vigorous: normal breathing, HR and tone. NG235 says do not suction before the shoulders are born, and do not suction or intubate a baby with normal breathing, HR and tone, whatever the meconium. The midwife stops the student, dries Amani and gives him to his mother skin-to-skin. Because the meconium was thick, this is significant meconium: Amani is observed at 1 and 2 hours, then 2-hourly to 12 hours, in a unit with immediate neonatologist access.

teach.text: Two different observation schedules: significant MECONIUM = 1 h, 2 h, then 2-hourly until 12 h; membranes ruptured MORE THAN 24 HOURS before established labour = 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours. And no antibiotics for prolonged rupture alone if mother and baby show no signs of infection.

items: Apgar at 1 and 5 minutes; colour by looking inside the mouth and at the nail beds.
Skin-to-skin, dry and cover, airway supported; no routine separation in the first hour.
First breastfeed ideally within 1 hour; weigh and measure head after the first hour.
Meconium: no suction before shoulders, none if vigorous; significant meconium observed 1 h, 2 h, then 2-hourly to 12 h.
Escalate: RR over 60, grunting, HR under 100 or over 160, CRT over 3 s, temp 38 C+, sats under 95%, central cyanosis.

summary: You can now support a newborn's transition with warmth, skin-to-skin, airway care and an early feed, and score the Apgar correctly. You can also follow the NICE rules on meconium and on observing babies after prolonged rupture of membranes, and know which findings need a neonatologist.

A.q: At what times does NICE NG235 recommend recording the Apgar score for all births?
options: At birth and 10 minutes
At 1 and 5 minutes
At 5 and 10 minutes
At 1, 5 and 15 minutes
A.why: NG235 1.11.1: record the Apgar score routinely at 1 minute and 5 minutes for all births.

whyNot.0: NICE specifies 1 and 5 minutes, not birth and 10 minutes.
whyNot.2: The first routine Apgar is at 1 minute.
whyNot.3: A 15-minute score is not part of the routine NICE recommendation.

A.q: How should the midwife assess central oxygenation for the colour element of the Apgar score?
options: By the colour of the hands and feet
By the colour of the face and lips
By the colour of the nail beds
By looking inside the mouth
A.why: NG235 1.11.2: assess central oxygenation by looking inside the mouth at the mucous membranes and tongue; peripheral oxygenation by the nail beds. This is more reliable across skin tones.

whyNot.0: Blue hands and feet (acrocyanosis) reflect peripheral circulation, not central oxygenation.
whyNot.1: Skin colour of the face is less reliable, particularly in babies with darker skin.
whyNot.2: The nail beds show peripheral, not central, oxygenation.

A.q: Lerato, 25, has just given birth and holds her baby skin-to-skin. When does NICE recommend breastfeeding should begin?
options: As soon as possible, ideally within 1 hour
Once the baby has been weighed and bathed
After the first set of newborn observations
Within 6 hours, once the mother has rested
A.why: NG235 1.11.11: encourage initiation of breastfeeding as soon as possible after the birth, ideally within 1 hour.

whyNot.1: Routine weighing and bathing should not separate mother and baby in the first hour (1.11.10).
whyNot.2: Observations should not delay the first feed in a well baby.
whyNot.3: Waiting 6 hours is far later than NICE recommends.

B.q: Baby Rhys is born through thick, dark green meconium. He is crying with good tone and HR 150. What should the midwife do about his airway?
options: Suction the oropharynx before the shoulders are born
Intubate and suction below the cords
Avoid suction; dry him and give skin-to-skin
Suction the nose and mouth once he is born
B.why: NG235 1.11.25: do not suction before birth of the shoulders and trunk, and do not suction or intubate if the baby has normal respiration, heart rate and tone.

whyNot.0: NICE advises against suction before birth of the shoulders and trunk.
whyNot.1: Intubation is not indicated when breathing, HR and tone are normal.
whyNot.3: Upper airway suction is not recommended for a vigorous baby.

B.q: After significant meconium, Baby Rhys is well. How often should he be observed?
options: 1 h, 2 h, then 2-hourly to 12 h
At 1 hour and 2 hours of age
At 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours of age
Hourly for the first 24 hours of life
B.why: NG235 1.11.27: after significant meconium in a healthy baby, observe at 1 and 2 hours, then 2-hourly until 12 hours, in a unit with immediate access to a neonatologist.

whyNot.1: 1 and 2 hours is the schedule for non-significant meconium (1.11.28).
whyNot.2: 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours is the schedule after prolonged rupture of membranes (1.11.31).
whyNot.3: Hourly observation for 24 hours is not the NICE schedule.

B.q: Baby Iris, 3 hours old, was born through non-significant meconium. Her RR is 68 and she is grunting. Her mother is at home after a home birth. What should the midwife do?
options: Repeat observations in 1 hour
Offer a feed and recheck in 30 minutes
Record it and inform the GP in the morning
Neonatologist review; transfer them both
B.why: NG235 1.11.29: after any degree of meconium, RR above 60 or grunting means ask a neonatologist to assess the baby; transfer both woman and baby if at home or in a freestanding midwifery unit.

whyNot.0: These findings need a neonatologist now; waiting an hour is unsafe.
whyNot.1: Feeding a grunting, tachypnoeic baby delays assessment and may be unsafe.
whyNot.2: Next-day GP review is far too slow for respiratory distress.

C.q: Bea's membranes ruptured 30 hours before established labour. She is well and apyrexial and her baby is well at birth. Which plan for the baby follows NICE NG235?
options: Start IV antibiotics for the baby straight away
Blood cultures and CRP before discharge
Routine observations at 1 and 2 hours
Observe at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours; no antibiotics
C.why: NG235 1.11.31-1.11.32: observe babies born after prelabour rupture of membranes more than 24 hours before established labour for 12 hours (at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours). With no signs of infection in woman or baby, do not give antibiotics.

whyNot.0: Antibiotics are not given if neither woman nor baby shows signs of infection.
whyNot.1: Do not perform blood or other culture tests in an asymptomatic baby (1.11.35).
whyNot.2: 1 and 2 hours is the schedule after non-significant meconium, not prolonged rupture.

C.q: Zoe, 29, asks the midwife to weigh and bathe her baby straight away so she can send photos to family. The baby is well and skin-to-skin. What is the best response?
options: Delay both until the 1-hour observations are done
Refuse, because bathing is not allowed on day 1
Explain skin-to-skin benefits; she decides
Bathe the baby but delay weighing for an hour
C.why: NG235 1.11.10: avoid separating mother and baby within the first hour for routine procedures such as weighing, measuring and bathing, unless the woman requests them. The midwife explains the benefits so she can make an informed choice and respects it.

whyNot.0: NICE sets no rule tying weighing or bathing to the 1-hour observations; in the first hour these depend on her informed request (NG235 1.11.10).
whyNot.1: There is no rule banning bathing on day 1; the guidance is about avoiding routine separation in the first hour unless she requests it.
whyNot.3: Bathing is also a routine procedure that separates them in the first hour.

C.q: Baby Jonah is skin-to-skin 20 minutes after birth. The midwife notices his head has flopped forward with his chin on his chest while his mother is drowsy. What is the priority?
options: Move him to a cot to sleep safely
Reposition his head to open the airway
Wake the mother to start a feed
Record observations at 1 hour as planned
C.why: NG235 1.11.9: prioritise optimal airway positioning during skin-to-skin, supporting the head so the airway does not become obstructed, and explain to the woman and companion how to maintain the airway.

whyNot.0: Separation is not needed; the airway must be repositioned and skin-to-skin can continue safely.
whyNot.2: A feed does not address the immediate airway risk.
whyNot.3: Waiting for scheduled observations leaves the airway at risk now.

reteach.title: Breathe, warm, feed
reteach.question: Every newborn has three jobs in the first hour. What are they, and how does the midwife help with each?

blocks.body: BREATHE: assess breathing, heart rate and tone, score the Apgar at 1 and 5 minutes, keep the airway open in skin-to-skin, and do not suction a vigorous baby. WARM: dry, cover and keep skin-to-skin; aim for 36.5-37.5 C. FEED: first breastfeed ideally within an hour, with no routine separation for weighing or bathing.

blocks.text: Meconium does not mean suction. A vigorous baby (normal breathing, HR and tone) gets NO suction and NO intubation, however thick the meconium.

explain.body: Five signs scored 0-2: heart rate, respiratory effort, tone, reflex irritability and colour. Record at 1 and 5 minutes. Colour: look inside the mouth for central oxygenation and at the nail beds for peripheral.

test.q: What should be recorded alongside the Apgar score, according to NG235 1.11.3?
options: The weight before the first feed
Time from birth to regular breathing
The baby's blood glucose at 1 hour of age
The cord pH on every baby
test.why: NG235 1.11.3: record the time from birth to the onset of regular respirations.

whyNot.0: Weighing is after the first hour and is not linked to the Apgar.
whyNot.2: Routine glucose is for at-risk babies, not all babies.
whyNot.3: Paired cord gases are not taken routinely (1.11.5), only if the baby is born in poor condition.

explain.body: Skin-to-skin as soon as possible; dry and cover with a warm, dry towel. Normal newborn temperature 36.5-37.5 C. Check temperature is in the normal range. Avoid routine separation in the first hour.

test.q: Which temperature range should the midwife aim to maintain in a newborn?
test.why: RCUK 2025: keep the newborn's temperature between 36.5 and 37.5 C.

whyNot.1: Below 36.5 C is hypothermia for a newborn.
whyNot.3: This range includes both cold and overheated values.

explain.body: No suction before shoulders and trunk; no suction or intubation if breathing, HR and tone are normal. Significant meconium: observe 1 h, 2 h, then 2-hourly to 12 h with neonatologist access. Non-significant: 1 h and 2 h.

test.q: Which finding after meconium requires a neonatologist to assess the baby?
options: Heart rate of 140 a minute
Respiratory rate of 50 a minute
Temperature of 37.0 C
Capillary refill of 4 s
test.why: NG235 1.11.29: capillary refill time above 3 seconds is one of the findings that need neonatologist assessment.

whyNot.0: HR 140 is within the normal range (escalate under 100 or over 160).
whyNot.2: 37.0 C is normal (escalate at 38 C or 37.5 C twice).

explain.body: If membranes ruptured more than 24 hours before established labour, observe the baby at 1, 2, 6 and 12 hours: temperature, HR, RR, grunting, recession, nasal flare, central cyanosis, capillary refill, floppiness, feeding. No antibiotics or cultures if there are no signs of infection.

test.q: For how long should women whose membranes ruptured over 24 hours before labour be told to report concerns about their baby's wellbeing?
options: The first 24 hours
The first 72 hours
The first 5 days
The first 6 weeks
test.why: NG235 1.11.34: advise women with prelabour rupture of membranes to report any concerns about their baby in the first 5 days, particularly the first 12 hours when infection risk is greatest.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is shorter than the 5 days NICE advises.
whyNot.1: 72 hours is the early-onset infection window in NG195, not this advice period.
whyNot.3: 6 weeks is longer than the NG235 advice.
